quote: Wie schliessen sich die Elemente an einander?
english: How do the elements connect to one another?
topic: Hilbert discusses solving Pfaffian-type differential equations without integrals (the 'diophantine' problem) by expressing the unknowns as functions of arbitrary functions and their derivatives, compares this to genus-0 algebraic relations, and considers transcendental relations between pairs of functions defined by partial differential or integral equations.

triage.modern_statement: Most likely this is about integrating underdetermined ODE/Pfaffian systems 'without integrals'. In Monge's sense, the unknowns are written in closed form as functions of arbitrary functions and finitely many of their derivatives. The note seems to ask how the 'elements' fit together into solutions (possibly integral or contact elements along a solution curve). The question is only one line, though, so no precise mathematical statement can be reconstructed from it. The broader topic on the page is clear: when does an underdetermined system admit such an integral-free general solution? Today this is called the Monge problem, and in control theory, differential flatness.
triage.answered_by: The specific question can't be linked to any answer. The page's broader topic was published by Hilbert himself in 'Über den Begriff der Klasse von Differentialgleichungen' (Math. Ann. 73, 1912). It was then developed by É. Cartan in 1914 (Bull. SMF 42) and later became the theory of differential flatness (Fliess, Lévine, Martin, Rouchon, 1990s onward).

evidence.claim: Hilbert published 'Über den Begriff der Klasse von Differentialgleichungen', Math. Ann. 73 (1912), pp. 95–108.
Cartan's 1914 Bull. SMF paper responds to Hilbert's article on the class of differential equations.
Flatness goes back to Hilbert's 1912 work on the general solution of Monge equations, which Cartan extended in 1914.
Recent research (Adv. Math. 2015) still cites Hilbert's and Cartan's papers on closed-form integration of underdetermined ODE systems.
Modern work on necessary and sufficient conditions for differential flatness links the topic to Hilbert's 22nd problem.
